israel-election-arab-parties.headline: Arab parties could hold the balance of power in Israel's election
israel-election-arab-parties.body_md:
Israel votes on Tuesday 27 October, the date set by law four years after the November 2022 election. The arithmetic is as old as the state's coalition politics: the Knesset has 120 seats, and a government needs 61. This time, neither of the two main blocs looks likely to get there with Jewish-led parties alone, and that puts a set of parties that both sides have long kept at arm's length in a position to decide the outcome.

## A stalemate on paper

Polling averages cited in late October put Binyamin Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition each at about 51 seats, with a few seats' difference depending on the survey and the window. One outlier poll gave the Netanyahu camp 62. The opposition is led, in most polls, by Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief, whose new Yashar party is running roughly level with Likud. Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid are running together on a joint list that polls well behind both.

The outgoing Knesset shows how close the margin is. Netanyahu's coalition held 60 seats when parliament dissolved, one short of a majority. The opposition held 59, plus one unaffiliated seat. Neither side has been able to find the extra seat.

That leaves roughly 18 seats outside the two blocs in the polling averages. Most belong to the Arab parties, which have generally been polling between about 10 and 13 seats in total, and the remainder to small lists hovering near the 3.25 per cent threshold. Votes for any party below that line are discarded, which can move the final arithmetic by several seats. A bloc's gain from a rival's wasted votes can matter as much as any swing in support.

## What the Arab parties hold

In 2022 the Arab parties won 10 seats between them: five for Ra'am and five for the Hadash-Ta'al alliance. That was down from 15 for the Joint List in 2020, when the four parties then in that alliance ran together. The fall followed a split, and many Arab voters stayed home. Turnout in Arab communities is the main variable this year. When it dips, the Arab parties lose seats, and the arithmetic shifts toward whichever bloc the Arab vote was never going to help.

Hadash and Ta'al have re-formed the Joint List with Balad for this election, while Ra'am, the Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas, runs separately. Ra'am has generally polled between four and six seats, close to its 2022 result.

The campaign has also tested whether they would be allowed to run at all. In September the Central Elections Committee, a body made up of party representatives, voted 15-8 to bar the Joint List after a petition from Likud, and voted to exclude Ra'am as well. It also blocked Sami Abu Shehadeh, Balad's chair. The petition relied on Basic Law provisions that bar parties backing armed struggle against Israel or negating its existence as a Jewish and democratic state. The committee's chair, Noam Sohlberg, a deputy president of the Supreme Court, and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara opposed excluding the parties. On 2 October the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the bans on the parties, finding that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold for exclusion. Abu Shehadeh withdrew after the court signalled that a majority of its judges would uphold his disqualification.

## The 2021 precedent

The question of whether an Arab party can sit in government is not hypothetical. In 2021 Ra'am, with four seats, joined the coalition of Bennett and Lapid, the first time an Arab party had been part of an Israeli government. The coalition, which spanned the right, centre and left, lasted about a year before collapsing in 2022. Its brief life is cited by both sides: by supporters as proof that the arrangement can work, and by Netanyahu's camp as proof that it cannot hold.

The present positions leave little room. Most Jewish-led opposition leaders have ruled out joining forces with Arab parties, and reporting this month says both Netanyahu and Bennett have publicly rejected governments that depend on Arab party support. Four leading opposition parties have signed a declaration not to attack each other before the vote and to cooperate afterwards. It does not extend to the Arab parties.

There is a distinction in Israeli coalition arithmetic that campaign rhetoric tends to blur. A party can be in a government, or it can merely deny the other side a majority by holding seats that cannot be counted on. If the Arab parties win 10 or more seats and the Jewish-led opposition falls short of 61 without them, an opposition government would need either their formal entry, their outside support in confidence votes, or their abstention. Their seats also shrink the pool the right needs, so Netanyahu's route to 61 is narrower the larger the Arab vote.

## What to watch

The first signal will be turnout, especially in Arab towns, and whether the small lists near the threshold clear it. Final results follow within days. The president then consults party leaders before choosing who is asked to try to form a government, and that stage is where the stated rejections of Arab support will meet the arithmetic. If no one reaches 61 and the Arab parties are held at arm's length by both sides, the likelier result is not a government but another round of coalition talks, and possibly another election.

tory-candidate-suspended.headline: Tories suspend former candidate over contract-killing claims
tory-candidate-suspended.body_md:
The Conservative Party has suspended a former local election candidate after an Al Jazeera undercover documentary appeared to show him discussing the price of hiring contract killers. The man is Jack Ross, chief executive of the campaign group Turning Point UK (TPUK). He denies the programme's findings. Police Scotland is assessing the footage, and the party's own inquiry has only just begun.

## What the documentary alleges

The film, *Contract Killers and the Far Right*, was reported by the Guardian on 21–22 October. It says Ross, apparently filmed by an undercover reporter, asked what the reporter wanted done and then set out options running from assault to killing, with prices. One report put the sums discussed at up to £50,000. The Guardian account says he offered to "broker" the services of a Glasgow-based man described as having alleged links to the Ulster Volunteer Force, a loyalist paramilitary group. That man is not named. The same man is said to have offered killings, including a hit-and-run made to look like drink-driving.

Some of the quoted remarks are blunt. Ross is reported as saying: "They can shoot someone. They can kill someone." He is also said to have told the reporter he would need to "keep my name out of it" if there was "lashback", and to have warned that journalists could hand recordings to police. The film further alleges that he was paid by Zimbabwean interests to organise a staged rally in favour of lifting sanctions.

Sources disagree on when the footage was recorded. One account says 2022, another that the investigation began in 2021, when a reporter joined TPUK as a videographer. No account found for this article says the programme shows a killing being commissioned or carried out.

## Suspension and denial

A Conservative spokesperson said: "Mr Ross's membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation." Ross stood as a Conservative in local elections. The reports do not say which ward or year, and that detail matters for judging what vetting the party did at the time.

Al Jazeera reports that Ross "completely" denies its findings and says nothing he told the undercover reporter was meant seriously. The Guardian approached him through TPUK. No response from the organisation is included in the version of the article available to this writer.

Police Scotland said it is aware of the documentary and will review and assess it "for any criminality". That is a statement about assessment only. It is not an investigation announced, a suspect named or a charge brought.

## The wider cast

The Guardian also reports on TPUK's chief operating officer, Nick Tenconi, who is filmed outlining a plan to use football hooligans to stir up trouble. He attended the 2022 Conservative conference with Ross. There is no suggestion in the material reviewed that the party knew of any of this at the time, but the overlap will draw questions about who was admitted to its events and on whose invitation.

## What the case does and does not show

The suspension is a holding measure. Parties commonly use it when allegations are serious and the facts are unsettled, and it implies no finding. The case rests, so far, on one broadcaster's covert filming, a published denial that the words were serious, and a police review at its earliest stage. Talk of a plot, as opposed to talk, is not supported by anything public.

The vetting question is real but narrower than it may look. Ross was a local candidate whose alleged conduct was filmed after, or around, his candidacy. Whether the party could have known depends on dates not yet established.

Two things will settle how large the story becomes: whether Police Scotland moves from review to investigation, and what the Conservatives' inquiry concludes about Ross and his association with the party. Neither has a published timetable.

sentencing-no-show-sanctions.headline: Offenders who skip sentencing to face solitary confinement or loss of visits
sentencing-no-show-sanctions.body_md:
The UK government is bringing into force powers to punish defendants who refuse to attend their own sentencing hearings. Offenders who stay in their cells rather than face the court can now expect to be held in solitary confinement or to lose social visits. The reported sanctions treat non-attendance as a matter for the prison regime, not only for the court.

The detail of the start date should be read with care. The reporting available to this desk is mostly from the bill stage in 2025, and it does not confirm the date on which the sanctions begin to be applied in practice.

## Why the law changed

The measure grew out of a run of cases in which convicted offenders declined to come up from the cells. The best known is Lucy Letby, who refused to attend even by video link while bereaved families read their victim personal statements at Manchester Crown Court. The judge passed a whole life order in her absence. Thomas Cashman and Koci Selamaj also stayed away from their sentencings.

Victims' families said the absence denied them the chance to address the offender and see the sentence delivered. Ministers took the view that a defendant should not be able to dodge that moment by simply declining to leave their cell.

## What the Victims and Courts Act provides

The provisions are in the Victims and Courts Act 2026, which was introduced as a bill in 2025. The first section inserts a new chapter into the Sentencing Code. It lets the Crown Court order a convicted person held in custody to attend sentencing. Failing to comply "without reasonable excuse" can be treated as criminal contempt.

The Law Gazette reported that the court can also impose "prison sanctions" modelled on existing prison disciplinary measures. These include loss of privileges, deductions from earnings and solitary confinement. Other coverage mentioned removal of access to the gym. Prison staff may use "reasonable force" on adult offenders to get them to the dock or the video link.

When the bill was announced, coverage also said judges could add up to two years to a sentence for refusing to attend. Sources disagreed on the scope. Some said the extra jail time applied only where the maximum sentence is life imprisonment. Others said the measure could apply to any Crown Court case. The loss of social visits, as described in this week's reporting, was not mentioned in the bill-stage material I reviewed.

## The objections

The Prison Reform Trust has called the measures disproportionate and unnecessary, arguing that existing law and policy already cover the problem. It warned of unintended consequences for prison safety, and it was particularly concerned about people who arrive in custody with sanctions already attached, especially in their first days. Practitioners writing in the Law Gazette have also argued that forced attendance is "no panacea".

There is a practical question underneath. Isolation and the loss of family contact are among the harshest tools a prison has. Using them to compel a court appearance moves them from managing behaviour inside the prison to enforcing a duty owed to the court.

## What to watch

The first test will be how often judges use the sanctions and how long they last. Whether any are challenged on proportionality grounds will also matter. Ministry of Justice guidance to prisons on applying them is the next document to look for.

php-vulnerability-global-alert.headline: Critical PHP flaw prompts global cyber alert and outages
php-vulnerability-global-alert.body_md:
A flaw in the software that runs most of the web's server-side code has set off emergency patching across several continents. Reuters, as cited by Krebs on Security, reported that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on the day of disclosure. The bug is not in any one website. It is in PHP itself, the language underneath WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento and a great many bespoke sites.

The picture is still incomplete. Several early claims about the episode do not survive a check against primary reporting, and the gap between what is known and what is being said is part of the story.

## What was found

The PHP project released fixes on 20–21 October (CyberScoop dates the release to Wednesday 20 October, while Krebs and others date it to the 21st) for two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The flaws have been nicknamed "PHP2Shell". Both score 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale, which tops out at 10, and both can allow an attacker to run code on a server without logging in. The fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35.

CyberScoop reports that the security firm Calif found the bug using an OpenAI model, while Wiz independently discovered and reported it. The two firms and OpenAI then spent roughly two months working with PHP maintainers on verification and disclosure. Watchtowr said the release had been scheduled for Thursday under embargo, and PHP brought it forward a day.

Because the flaw sits in the runtime, a site is exposed even if its own code is clean. Wiz describes memory-safety bugs that sat in the code for decades and were hard to exploit. Wiz also argues that AI tools lower the effort of adapting such exploits, and compared the situation with Log4Shell in 2021.

## How big is the exposure?

Estimates vary. CyberScoop puts PHP's share at 70–80% of sites with a known server-side language. Researchers there estimate more than 1.3 million internet-exposed hosts could be vulnerable, and a Shodan search counted about 1.9 million. Censys, cited by Krebs, counts about 2.58 million internet-facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

The older installations are the worry. VirusTotal data cited by CyberScoop shows about 758,000 servers that disclose their version run branches from 5.4 through 8.1, which no longer receive security updates. Only about 272,000 run supported branches. For the first group there is no official patch, only migration. CERT-EU said the flaws could affect every version from PHP 5 onward, though neither the technical cause nor a full list of affected versions had been officially confirmed.

Whether the flaws are being exploited is disputed. Qualys reports exploitation attempts in the wild, and Krebs says experts report working exploits. CISA said it had not observed exploitation at the time of publication, and CyberScoop found mostly reconnaissance, with Huntress unable to confirm a successful compromise on customer systems. Code claiming to exploit the flaws is circulating and is unverified. Security firms warn that such code can itself carry malware.

## The coordination gap

The triage premise for this piece was that Washington was coordinating a fix, with the US notified on 16 October. Neither claim could be confirmed. No source found names 16 October as a notification date. Krebs gives no disclosure date at all. The US role visible in the record is CISA's public advisory, which says the flaws "pose a risk to organizations if left unpatched". CERT-EU and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre issued similar guidance to prepare to update quickly and to isolate internet-facing applications where immediate patching is not feasible. Those are advisories, not a coordinated fix. The fix came from PHP's maintainers.

That is the real shape of the problem. A shared open-source component, maintained by a small project, was patched through a private effort among a few companies. National agencies then had to work out their own exposure after the public release. Government sites are no different from any other PHP deployment: they run the same runtime, often on the same old branches. Krebs, which discloses that Wiz advertises on its site, says nearly 70% of websites need to update core software and that many may show error pages while they do.

There is also a data problem. The outage reports so far come from secondhand accounts. Beinsure reported maintenance-related outages at some services, but neither it nor the organisations involved had confirmed any link to the PHP flaws. The count of affected public services is unknown.

## What to watch

Three things will settle this. First, whether CISA's known-exploited catalog adds either CVE, which would move the claim of exploitation from rumour to record. Second, the pace of patching on the roughly 758,000 servers running unsupported branches, where no vendor fix exists. Third, whether the governments whose sites went down publish what they ran and how long it took to update. Until then, the scale of this episode rests on estimates of exposure rather than a measured count of damage.

just-eat-ai-apology.headline: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after online ridicule
just-eat-ai-apology.body_md:
Just Eat has apologised after AI-generated food content on its platform drew ridicule online. The company's mistakes were spotted and mocked in public, and the apology followed. The episode says less about what the technology can do than about how little room a consumer brand has when it publishes machine-made material without close checking.

The account rests on a single report, from BBC Technology. That report is thin on detail. It does not make clear which content was affected, how many errors there were, or what Just Eat has changed since. Those gaps limit what can responsibly be said here, and nothing below goes beyond what has been reported.

## What happened

The sequence is simple. Just Eat put out AI-generated food content, and it contained errors. People noticed and shared examples on social media, where they were widely laughed at. The company then apologised.

The speed matters more than the specifics. A mistake in a brochure or a printed menu might sit unnoticed for weeks. A mistake on a platform used by millions can be screenshotted, shared and mocked within hours. The correction, in this case, came from the public rather than from internal review. The apology came after the ridicule, not before it.

## A brand problem, not a breakthrough

It is tempting to file this under AI failure. That framing is too generous to the story and too harsh on the technology. Generative systems are known to produce confident errors, and any company using them for customer-facing material knows this. Food is an especially unforgiving subject: customers can see at a glance when a picture or a description doesn't match a dish they recognise.

The risk lies in the process around the tool. If the content went live without a human checking it, the failure was one of review, not of software. The reporting does not say whether that was the case, so that point remains open. What can be said is that the cost fell on the brand, in the form of public embarrassment and an apology it would have preferred not to issue.

## What it signals

For companies deploying generative AI in customer-facing content, this is a small but clear data point. Errors will be found by customers, quickly and in public, and the response is expected to be fast. The saving from producing content cheaply can be wiped out by a single viral example.

It also raises the bar for what an apology needs to contain. A statement that says sorry but names no fix invites the next round of mockery. The reported coverage does not yet say what Just Eat will do differently, whether that means more human checking, narrower use of the tools, or removal of the content in question.

## What to watch

The test is whether Just Eat explains what went wrong and what it has changed, and whether further errors surface in its content afterwards. Other delivery and retail platforms using AI-generated listings and images will be watching how this plays out. If the company publishes details, the BBC report is where they are most likely to appear first.
just-eat-ai-apology.in_one_sentence: Just Eat apologised after errors in its AI-generated food content were mocked online, a brand-reputation lesson more than a technology story.

donaldson-parliament-investigation.headline: Jeffrey Donaldson investigated over alleged rape inside Parliament
donaldson-parliament-investigation.body_md:
The Metropolitan Police are investigating an allegation that Jeffrey Donaldson, the former leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, raped a woman inside the Palace of Westminster. The allegation is unproven and no charges have been brought. It reaches the capital's police at a point when Donaldson is already in prison for other offences.

## What the Met has said

The force said it received a report on 13 October from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI). It describes an alleged rape in 2016 involving one victim, who is being supported by specialist officers. The Met called the inquiry early-stage. No arrests have been made and enquiries are continuing.

Its statement did not name Donaldson. The link comes from media reporting. A woman from Northern Ireland was reportedly interviewed by PSNI officers, who then passed their information to London. Because the alleged offence is said to have happened on the parliamentary estate, the Met rather than the PSNI would lead any investigation.

The Belfast Telegraph reported in July that a woman said Donaldson sexually assaulted her in the DUP's parliamentary offices after a tour in 2016. She said he tried to kiss her and put his hand up her skirt. The BBC later reported that the same woman also alleges he raped her. Outlets differ slightly on details, and the allegation has not been tested in any court.

## The existing case

Donaldson, who led the DUP until he resigned in March 2024, was convicted in June of historical sex offences against two girls. The offences ran from 1985 to 2008. He was convicted of 18 offences: one count of rape, 13 of indecent assault and four of gross indecency. He was sentenced to 15 years. He has been stripped of his knighthood and removed from the Privy Council. His solicitor has said an appeal has been lodged.

The new allegation is separate from those convictions. Any new prosecution would have to be decided on its own evidence, and he is presumed innocent of it.

## Why the setting matters

Westminster has spent years trying to repair how it handles complaints of misconduct. It created an independent complaints and grievance scheme after the 2017 revelations, and it has been criticised since for being slow and opaque. A serious sexual allegation said to have taken place in an MP's workplace is a test of that machinery, even though this one is going through the police and not the parliamentary process.

The period also matters. The alleged incident dates from 2016, when Donaldson was a sitting MP. Parliament will presumably be asked what records, such as pass logs and CCTV, still exist from that time. Nothing in the public reporting says what evidence the Met has.

## What to watch

The next step is whether the Met moves from an early-stage inquiry to interviewing Donaldson, who is in custody, and then passes a file to the Crown Prosecution Service. Separately, the outcome of his appeal against the June convictions is still pending. Neither has a published timetable.
donaldson-parliament-investigation.in_one_sentence: The Met is investigating an unproven allegation that jailed ex-DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson raped a woman in Parliament in 2016; no arrests or charges so far.

no10-ai-adviser-role.headline: No 10 advertises for an adviser on AI's effect on citizens
no10-ai-adviser-role.body_md:
Downing Street is hiring, and the job title says a good deal about what it thinks it has to deal with. A Guardian Politics report says No 10 is advertising for an adviser to help citizens cope with the rise of artificial intelligence. A job advert is not a policy. It is still the first visible sign that the centre of government wants its own people working on how AI lands on ordinary lives, as distinct from how AI is regulated or how the technology sector is courted.

## What is known, and what is not

The detail is thin. The Guardian's headline sets out the remit: an adviser on AI's effect on citizens. The material available for this piece did not include the salary, the start date, the grade, the reporting line or the job specification, and the advert's text could not be independently checked. Everything below about what the post means is therefore inference, not reporting.

That gap matters because the same title can describe two very different jobs. One is a senior policy post with a brief to shape decisions on work, public services, online harms and the welfare state. The other is a communications-and-engagement role, whose holder explains to the public what the government is already doing. The first would suggest a standing policy workstream. The second would suggest a government that wants to be seen to have an answer.

## Signals to look for

The advert's wording is the best test. Several features would point towards substance:

- **Reporting line.** A post reporting to the Prime Minister's policy unit or the Cabinet Office carries more weight than one in a press office.
- **Grade and pay.** A special-adviser or senior civil service salary band implies a seat in decision-making. A junior band implies support work.
- **Verbs in the job description.** "Advise on" and "shape" mean something different from "promote" and "communicate".
- **Who it works with.** Links to the AI Security Institute, the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and the departments that deal with benefits, jobs and schools would suggest cross-government reach.

No 10 already has AI expertise nearby. Trade press has reported that Jade Leung was appointed the Prime Minister's AI adviser, splitting her time between the AI Security Institute and Downing Street. That post is concerned with frontier-model safety. A role on citizens would cover different ground, namely the everyday consequences of AI for jobs, services and public trust. If the new post sits alongside the existing one, it would suggest that government sees AI as having a public-impact side as well as a security side. That reading is plausible but unconfirmed.

## Why it matters

British AI policy has so far leaned towards investment, growth and safety testing of the most powerful models. The public-facing questions have been left to individual departments. These include what happens to entry-level jobs, how automated decisions are challenged, and what people are told when a chatbot is making the call. A dedicated adviser in No 10 would be an attempt to give those questions an owner. The same concerns are surfacing elsewhere in today's news, from [AI firms warning of local opposition to datacentres](/article/uk-datacentre-protests-warning) to [a food-delivery firm apologising for AI mistakes](/article/just-eat-ai-apology).

A caution is in order. Governments advertise advisory posts far more readily than they fund the policy work behind them. One hire does not amount to a department, a budget or a legislative plan. Until the advert's text is read in full and the appointee's remit becomes clear, this is a hiring signal, not evidence of a policy shift.

## What to watch

The closing date and the eventual appointment will be the first real data points. The next is whether the post's remit shows up in published government work on AI and employment, or in any public-facing AI strategy. If it does, the advert was an early marker of a standing workstream. If it does not, it may stay an advert.
no10-ai-adviser-role.in_one_sentence: Downing Street is advertising for an adviser on AI's effect on citizens, but without the job spec it is a hiring signal, not proof of a policy shift.

connectwise-ai-supply-chain-attack.headline: Microsoft says China-aligned hackers used AI to speed ConnectWise supply-chain attack
connectwise-ai-supply-chain-attack.body_md:
A company that manages IT for other companies is a convenient thing to break into. Get inside it once and you inherit its relationships. Microsoft says that is what a China-aligned hacking group did to ConnectWise, a major supplier of software to managed service providers (MSPs). It also says the group used an AI tool to move faster than defenders usually expect.

Microsoft disclosed the findings on Wednesday. It attributes the compromise of the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application to a group it tracks as Storm-0940, which it describes as China state-aligned. It says the group used an agentic AI penetration-testing framework called ARTEX against hundreds of organisations from September 2026. The AI-acceleration claim is Microsoft's own assessment. It has not been independently verified, and this account draws on reporting of Microsoft's disclosure rather than on a full reading of the primary document. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to Reuters. Beijing routinely denies conducting or condoning cyber-enabled theft.

## How the attack worked

Microsoft's account is not that the AI found some novel exploit. It describes AI agents speeding up familiar, unglamorous steps: scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and the abuse of OAuth applications, the permissioned connections that let one cloud service act inside another.

The pattern in Microsoft's telemetry is specific. Between 10 and 14 October, infrastructure at a single IP address ran an automated cross-tenant password-spray campaign against 327 accounts at eight organisations, aiming at Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online. Microsoft logged more than 151,000 failed sign-ins. The peak came on 11 October, at 2,900 failures a minute, with over 111,000 failures that day. Forty-eight accounts took more than 1,000 failures each. Microsoft says it saw no successful authentication, token issuance or directory change in that window.

Then, on 15 October, the pattern shifted. Microsoft says AI agents gained control of the identities of several ConnectWise cloud applications and used them to sign in to customer environments. That route needs no user password. The attackers relied on the trust each customer had already granted the application. Microsoft says the actor attempted to sign in to more than 2,250 tenants.

Where access worked, the agents moved on to Microsoft Graph, the interface for reading and changing a tenant's directory, and carried out what Microsoft calls "AI-accelerated follow-on activity": reconnaissance, application credential changes, and changes to identities, groups and privileged roles. Microsoft warns that those credential changes "can remain active as a backdoor even after the original compromised application" is cleaned up.

## The speed claim

The claim that matters most is about time. Microsoft says ARTEX "accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse" and that some attacks reached privileged access in cloud infrastructure within three hours of initial targeting. It adds that "agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans."

A few caveats apply. Three hours is fast, but Microsoft's material, as reported, does not give a human-operated baseline for the same attacks, so how much time the AI actually saved is not established. Reuters reports that most of the targeting was unsuccessful, though Microsoft said the group quickly gained privileged cloud persistence at many organisations. Nor is the tool itself simple to describe. Reuters calls ARTEX open-source and able to work with any AI model. The Hacker News says it was made closed-source after being abused against South Korean financial institutions. The sources disagree on that point.

The targeting was broad: aerospace and defence, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductors, software, technology, think tanks and non-profits. That fits Storm-0940's profile. Microsoft first described the group in November 2024, tied to a botnet called Quad7 used for evasive password spraying, and assesses it has been active since at least 2021.

## Why the supply chain is the point

The supply-chain route is what turns a single breach into hundreds. An MSP or software vendor holds standing access to many customers, and customers extend that access because it saves them work. Defenders have traditionally had some slack in that arrangement: the gap between an attacker getting in and fanning out was long enough to notice things. If agents can test every downstream connection at machine speed, that slack shrinks.

ConnectWise's chief executive, Manny Rivelo, said: "it appears that a China state-aligned group was responsible for the attack on ConnectWise Cloud Backup." The company says it has contained the affected application connections and is restoring services in phases, a process it expects to take several days. It also cautioned that containment does not remove unauthorised access already established inside individual customer tenants, which each need separate review. In its statement ConnectWise said that "nation-state actors are increasingly targeting the software supply chain" and that "every vendor and every MSP must defend itself with both of those risks in mind."

## What to watch

The practical test is clean-up. Customers of ConnectWise Cloud Backup will need to audit OAuth applications for newly added credentials and review recent changes to privileged roles and groups, since those are the persistence mechanisms Microsoft describes. ConnectWise's phased restoration and its trust-site advisory will show how many customers turn out to have been touched. Independent confirmation of the timing claims from outside Microsoft would also help show whether AI is changing how quickly these attacks move or only how much of the routine work gets automated.
connectwise-ai-supply-chain-attack.in_one_sentence: Microsoft says China-aligned Storm-0940 used the ARTEX AI tool to speed a ConnectWise supply-chain compromise that targeted hundreds of organisations; the AI-speed claim is Microsoft's own.

uk-datacentre-protests-warning.headline: AI firms warn UK has a year to head off datacentre protests
uk-datacentre-protests-warning.body_md:
The companies that want to fill Britain with AI datacentres have told ministers they have about twelve months to win over the neighbours. If they don't, they say, the kind of local opposition that has stalled projects in the United States will start to threaten construction here.

The warning comes in a submission to the Labour government from the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce, whose members include Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco. It was first reported by the Guardian. It is an industry document with an industry interest, and it should be read that way. But the specific things it asks for show where the industry thinks the pressure points are.

## What the taskforce wants

SAIL says scrutiny of datacentres is rising because of repeated dry summers and higher energy bills. Datacentres draw heavily on both electricity and, for cooling, water. The submission argues that the deeper drivers are distrust of corporate and government promises, fear of stranded assets and electricity costs, and that these are now surfacing in Britain. It cites US experience, where it says organised opposition has "stopped fully permitted datacentre projects" and led to moratoriums.

Its proposals are mostly about money and process:

- A "compact" setting out how communities benefit from hosting datacentres.
- Letting host councils keep more of the tax revenue the sites generate, including business rates.
- A government framework for councils and mayors, with recommended local benefit terms.
- An indicative contribution from developers, in cash or facilities, scaled to the size of each site.

SAIL has not calculated what it would cost central government if councils kept all their business rates. Its chair, Steve Rigby, says the taskforce wants "high-impact actions" rather than another strategy document.

Microsoft, which has pledged $30bn (£22bn) for UK AI infrastructure, has built a datacentre in Acton, west London, and has another under construction in Newport. It wants to build several more and says it is talking to local and national leaders.

## The government's position

A government spokesperson said datacentres should create British jobs and supply chains, invest in the communities that host them, prioritise clean power and use water responsibly. Community benefits, they said, are already weighed through local planning processes. Ministers have also announced that councils hosting datacentres in England's AI growth zones can keep all the additional business rates those sites generate. That is close to what SAIL is asking for, though the taskforce wants it extended and given a framework.

## Campaigners are not persuaded

The people the industry is worried about take a different view. Joseph Miller, director of PauseAI UK, which campaigns for a global pause on datacentre expansion, said the firms are "absolutely right to be worried". He expects communities to see benefit payments as an attempt to buy them off.

Kat Jones, director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, said tech firms have already missed the chance to contain local opposition. She counts 15 community campaigns in Scotland and a growing national movement. The Guardian's piece carried a photograph of protesters opposing a datacentre in North Ayrshire.

Donald Campbell, director of advocacy at Foxglove, argued that big tech has relied on secrecy and misleading information in planning applications. Letting councils keep more business rates, he said, would cost central government money that might otherwise fund services such as the NHS, while the tech firms would "not pay a penny more".

## Why it matters

The dispute turns a technology question into a planning one. Capacity plans for AI depend on sites being approved, connected to the grid and supplied with water, and each of those happens locally. The industry is effectively conceding that its case is not yet made at that level, and is asking for public money, in the form of retained council tax revenue, to make it.

The evidence so far is thin on British specifics. The submission points to US precedent rather than to British projects that have been blocked, and the Guardian report names no UK scheme that has been cancelled. The twelve-month figure is the taskforce's own estimate, not a forecast anyone has tested.

What to watch is whether the government turns the retained-rates policy into the wider framework SAIL wants, and whether any planning application for a major site draws organised opposition of the kind campaigners say is already forming in Scotland. The cost to the Treasury, which SAIL has not worked out, is the figure that will decide how far ministers go.
uk-datacentre-protests-warning.in_one_sentence: An industry taskforce including Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco tells ministers they have about a year to win over local communities before US-style opposition threatens UK datacentre construction.

city-of-culture-2029-shortlist.headline: Four locations in the running for UK City of Culture 2029
city-of-culture-2029-shortlist.body_md:
Four places are still in the race to become UK City of Culture 2029, after the shortlist for the title was announced. The BBC reported the news. The competition runs every four years and rewards the winner with a year in the national spotlight.

This piece does not name the four finalists. The details available at filing were limited to the headline fact that the field has narrowed to four, and the shortlist should be checked against the BBC's report before anyone relies on it.

## What the title is worth

The UK City of Culture scheme was designed to use a year-long programme of events to pull in visitors, investment and civic confidence. The prize is rarely the headline grant. It is the platform: a year of national attention, a programme that local arts organisations can build on, and a reason for councils, universities and businesses to pull in the same direction.

That is why bids tend to be as much about regional ambition as about culture in the narrow sense. A place that reaches a shortlist has usually already won something, whether a stronger partnership between its local authorities and its arts sector or a clearer story about what it wants to become.

## What is not yet known

The figures that would turn this from a notice into a proper story are missing. There are no confirmed funding amounts, no detail of what each finalist is proposing, and no timetable for the final decision in the material available here. Each of those matters. A shortlist of four invites comparisons: coastal against inland, big city against smaller town, a place with a long cultural record against one making its first serious pitch. Without the names, those comparisons cannot be drawn honestly, and none is offered here.

## What to watch

The next milestone is the judges' assessment of the four bids and the announcement of the winner. Until then, the finalists will spend months making their case to a panel and to their own residents, whose support often counts for as much as the written bid. Once the names are confirmed, the questions to ask are how much money each bid commits to, how much of it is new, and what happens to the programme if the title goes elsewhere. For the three places that miss out, the plans written for the bid frequently survive it, and that is often the more lasting result.
city-of-culture-2029-shortlist.in_one_sentence: The shortlist for the UK City of Culture 2029 title has narrowed to four places, though the finalists' names and bid details still need confirming against the BBC report.

alzheimers-repurposing-trial.headline: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in UK study
alzheimers-repurposing-trial.body_md:
A new UK trial will test whether two medicines already in routine use, one for type 2 diabetes and one for ADHD, can slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease. The study, called AD-SMART, has begun treating its first participant. It has no results yet, so it is an announcement of a study and not evidence that either drug works against dementia.

## The drugs and the design

The first two compounds under test are metformin, a first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes, and atomoxetine, which is prescribed for ADHD. Reports of the launch say both may dampen inflammation in the brain, a process implicated in neurodegeneration. That is a hypothesis, and the trial exists to test it.

AD-SMART is described as a multi-arm study: several candidate drugs run side by side against a single shared placebo group. If one drug shows no benefit it can be dropped and replaced by another without starting a new trial from scratch. Organisers say this structure could roughly halve the time taken to evaluate treatments, with conclusions targeted for 2030. That timeline is the organisers' aim, not a forecast.

Coverage reports a target of 1,200 participants at more than 30 sites across the UK, with regular blood tests and scans to track progress. Angela Bucksey, 67, from Cambridgeshire, diagnosed in January, is reported as the first person to start treatment. The UK Dementia Research Institute and Alzheimer's Research UK are reported to lead the work, with government backing among other funding. Details such as the trial phase, dosing and the primary outcome measure were not available in the coverage reviewed, and the original BBC report could not be read directly; these figures come from secondary summaries and should be treated accordingly.

## Why repurpose?

Drugs already approved for another condition have known safety profiles and manufacturing routes, which can remove years and a large share of the cost from development. Alzheimer's Research UK has estimated that roughly a third of drugs in clinical trials for Alzheimer's are already used for other conditions, so the approach is well established.

The diabetes link in particular has a long, mixed history. Observational studies have associated some diabetes drugs with lower dementia risk; one analysis of about 110,000 people with type 2 diabetes linked SGLT-2 and DPP-4 inhibitors to a 35 per cent lower risk. Such designs cannot establish causation, because people prescribed one drug differ from those prescribed another in ways that are hard to measure. Experts reacting to those findings repeatedly called for randomised trials, which is what a placebo-controlled platform provides.

There is also a caution specific to this study. Patients with Alzheimer's are typically older and often take several other medicines, so side effects and interactions will matter as much as any cognitive signal. Whether metformin, which is taken by people with diabetes, behaves the same way in participants without it is an open question the trial design will have to address.

## What to watch

The first checkpoint is enrolment: whether the trial reaches its 1,200-person target and publishes its protocol and primary endpoints. Interim decisions to drop or add arms would be the earliest sign of how the platform is working. Any efficacy answer is not expected before the end of the decade.
alzheimers-repurposing-trial.in_one_sentence: A UK platform trial, AD-SMART, will test metformin and atomoxetine in Alzheimer's patients; it has just begun and has no results yet.

arsenal-bayern-draw-saka-injury.headline: Rice earns Arsenal a draw at Bayern, but Saka injury 'does not look good'
arsenal-bayern-draw-saka-injury.body_md:
Arsenal left Munich with a point, a late equaliser from Declan Rice and a worry. Bukayo Saka went off injured, and the early word on the winger, as relayed in the BBC Sport report, is that it "does not look good". The match finished 2-2 at the Allianz Arena on Wednesday night in the Champions League. Arsenal can be pleased with the draw, and Saka's injury is the larger concern.

## A game that swung twice

Bayern were the more threatening side for long spells, and one match report noted they will feel they should have won. Arsenal still took the lead first. Eberechi Eze, on as a substitute for the injured Saka, collected Martin Ødegaard's punt in behind and scored in the 25th minute. Alphonso Davies levelled before half-time, in the 35th.

The second half belonged to Harry Kane. Bayern's captain had a shot blocked by a handball from Arsenal's Timber, and he converted the penalty himself in the 61st minute. Kane has scored against Arsenal in this competition before, from the spot at the Emirates in April 2024. He did not need many chances to hurt them again.

## Rice finds the answer

Arsenal were behind with eight minutes left when Rice struck in the 82nd. Reports credit the build-up to Noni Madueke and Viktor Gyökeres. The goal rescued a point against a side that had looked likelier to take all three, and it keeps Arsenal in the mix in the league phase.

A point in Munich is a good result on its own terms. This one cost Arsenal their right winger.

## The Saka question

Saka's withdrawal came before Eze's goal, so the injury happened early. The source says it "does not look good", but no diagnosis or timescale had been published when this piece was written. The nature and length of the injury are unconfirmed and should be checked against the club's next update.

The cover is the question. Eze scored after replacing Saka, which shows he can fill the role. But Saka has been among Arsenal's most dependable attackers for years, and a long absence would stretch a squad that is also playing across several competitions. Madueke and Gyökeres both featured in the equaliser, so Arsenal have options in attack. Replacing Saka's output over a run of games is a different test from replacing him for 70 minutes.

## What next

The immediate catalyst is a medical assessment of Saka, which should settle whether this is a matter of days or months. Arsenal's next fixtures will show how Mikel Arteta rearranges the right side without him.

bevan-security-file-tame.headline: Aneurin Bevan's security file 'remarkably tame', National Archives shows
bevan-security-file-tame.body_md:
The state kept a file on Aneurin Bevan, and the file, it turns out, is not much to read. A release from the National Archives has put the NHS founder's security file into public view. The Guardian describes it as "remarkably tame".

That verdict will disappoint anyone hoping for a Cold War thriller. Bevan was the most combustible figure in the postwar Labour government. As Minister of Health from 1945 to 1951 he built the National Health Service, which opened in July 1948. He did it over the open hostility of much of the medical profession. He was also a standing provocation to the right, and he was plainly the kind of politician about whom a security service might be expected to keep notes. The surprise is how little the notes appear to contain.

## What the file does and does not say

The details of the release could not be independently confirmed for this article, so this account relies on the Guardian's characterisation. On that account, there are no revelations about surveillance of Bevan and no new light on how the state regarded him. The file does not change the picture of a politician who was watched, as many on the left were, but not obviously pursued.

Bevan's record was the sort that invited attention. He was a Welsh miner's son who rose through the South Wales coalfield and the Labour left. He was an outspoken critic of Conservative governments, and in the 1950s he led the left of his own party. Public controversy was never in short supply. Wartime and postwar records at Kew already hold much on his politics, including a 1942 War Cabinet memorandum on a newspaper article of his. A thin security file sits easily alongside all that: a record of a loud public figure whose views were hardly secret.

## A curiosity, not a correction

Archive releases of this kind make good copy when they overturn something. This one does the opposite. A dull file is a small piece of evidence that the machinery of watching was less interested in Bevan than his reputation might suggest. It is not strong evidence either way. A tame file is silent on what was kept elsewhere, what was destroyed, and what was never written down.

Bevan died in 1960, aged 62. The NHS he founded is the thing he is remembered for, and a modest folder at Kew adds nothing to that.

The next thing to watch is the catalogue entry itself. The National Archives' Discovery catalogue will show exactly what the file holds and which departments created it. Historians of the period can then test the Guardian's description against the pages.
bevan-security-file-tame.in_one_sentence: A National Archives release of Aneurin Bevan's security file finds it unremarkable, a small curiosity that adds little to the story of the NHS founder or of state surveillance.

north-sea-jackdaw-licences-standing-char.headline: Jackdaw approval, a Norway-style fund that never was, and gas standing charges: the North Sea fight
north-sea-jackdaw-licences-standing-char.body_md:
The government has approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea while leaving in place its ban on new oil and gas exploration licences. That combination is now the centre of a dispute that runs from the Green benches to the Conservative front bench. Critics call the approval "climate vandalism". Kemi Badenoch wants the licence ban overturned altogether.

The decision came on 21 October, according to [Novara Media](https://novaramedia.com/2026/10/21/burnham-approves-new-north-sea-gas-drilling-in-act-of-climate-vandalism/). Andy Burnham's government cleared the Shell and Equinor project. Burnham has defended the decision, arguing that it protects jobs and helps keep homes warm this winter, as [Oceanographic](https://oceanographicmagazine.com/news/uk-s-climate-ambition-in-tatters-as-jackdaw-gasfield-get-go-ahead/) reports. Critics dispute that it will lower bills.

## An approval, not a new policy

The distinction between approving a field and licensing new exploration is the whole of the government's position. Jackdaw is an existing, already-licensed development. It was first consented under the previous Conservative government. A Scottish court later found the consents unlawful because the emissions from burning the fuel had not been assessed. Approving it again is therefore a case-by-case decision on a project with a history, not a change to the licensing regime. Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge of no new oil and gas licences remains in force on the government's account.

The pledge has been under strain for weeks. Before the decision, Burnham had complained that approval of Jackdaw and Rosebank was delayed by "government process", as [City AM](https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465789) reported. [ITV News](https://www.itv.com/news/2026-10-11/tories-urge-burnham-to-stop-dithering-and-approve-jackdaw-and-rosebank) reported the Conservatives urging him to stop "dithering". Labour is reportedly split on the matter.

The reaction from the left was swift. Scottish Greens co-leader Ross Greer called it a "devastating betrayal of our children's future", per [STV News](https://news.stv.tv/north/climate-campaigners-angry-at-jackdaw-gas-field-approval). Greenpeace and Green Party of England and Wales leader Zack Polanski were also critical, according to the Novara and Oceanographic reports. Novara noted that Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh had opposed new drilling before taking the post.

## The Tory counter-offer

The Conservatives do not regard the approval as sufficient. Badenoch is pressing the government to overturn the ban on new licences, and her party also wants the Energy Profits Levy scrapped. Shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie has accused Burnham of "dithering and delaying".

That leaves the government with critics on both sides. For the Greens and campaigners, approving Jackdaw is already too much. For the Tories, approving single fields without a licensing round is too little. Whether the arrangement is stable is the question for the sector. UK-listed producers would find it easier to plan around a regime that approves tie-backs and existing developments than around one that revisits each project. The approvals do not open up new acreage, though, and the long-run reserves outlook still depends on the licensing ban.

## The fund that was never built

The argument has a counterfactual attached. A BBC piece asks what a Norway-style North Sea fund might be worth had Britain built one, and it puts the answer in the region of a trillion pounds. The BBC's methodology could not be checked for this article, and the figure should be treated as an illustrative counterfactual rather than a measured loss.

Other estimates are lower. The Institute for Public Policy Research has said that a fund built from North Sea tax receipts in the 1980s would now be worth over £500bn. It put those receipts at roughly £166bn between 1981 and 1990. The IPPR argued that the money went on cutting other taxes. Norway's own fund is now generally reported at over $2tn. The size of the gap depends heavily on the assumed revenue base and the period. The IPPR also concluded that the opportunity to capitalise a UK fund from North Sea revenue has passed.

The counterfactual feeds the licensing debate in both directions. Supporters of drilling say that remaining production should at least be taxed and used well. Opponents say the history shows that the revenue case for new fields is weaker than advertised.

## Bills: the standing-charge thread

Burnham is also pushing a bills argument. The BBC reports that he has proposed a plan to cut standing charges from gas bills. Earlier reporting in July said he was considering a plan drawn up by the Nesta think tank, which suggested savings of about £130 a year for the average household. The proposal would overhaul gas standing charges, which add about 29p a day regardless of usage, and shift some levies off energy bills.

The costings in the coverage conflict. One account says the standing-charge reform alone costs taxpayers nothing, while the wider package is put at £3.2bn a year. Households using more gas would pay more under the reform, and those using less would pay less. No government response, timetable or funding mechanism for the latest proposal could be confirmed. Until one appears, it remains positioning rather than policy, and the effect on suppliers such as Centrica cannot be assessed.

## What to watch

The next test is whether Rosebank follows Jackdaw. It faces the same legal history and the same Tory pressure, and a decision there would show whether case-by-case approval has become the settled approach. A legal challenge to Jackdaw would be a second marker. The earlier approvals were struck down on exactly that ground. The third is any formal Conservative commitment to reverse the licence ban before the Budget.

gcse-female-scientists.headline: Only one female scientist named in GCSE specifications, study finds
gcse-female-scientists.body_md:
Open a GCSE science specification and look for the names of the people who made the discoveries. In a new study of the documents that set what the exams can ask, one woman turns up at GCSE level. She is Rosalind Franklin, and she appears in just one specification.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge went through the specifications of the UK's six main exam boards. These are the official documents that tell teachers what students must learn and what papers may assess. They covered biology, chemistry, environmental science, geology, physics and astronomy. The study was published on 21 October in the *British Educational Research Journal*, under the title "The absence of women's scientific contributions in core UK pre-university science qualifications". The authors are Dr Greg J Cooke, Skyla B White and Stephanie Buttigieg, who worked with the IncludeHer movement.

## The numbers

At Key Stage 4, which covers GCSEs and equivalent qualifications, the specifications name 86 scientists. One is a woman: Franklin, whose X-ray work was central to working out the structure of DNA.

At Key Stage 5, covering A-levels and equivalents, the count is 181 scientists, of whom three are women. Franklin is joined by the geophysicist Marie Tharp and the seismologist Inge Lehmann.

The study looked at specifications, not textbooks or what teachers do in lessons. Teachers can and do add names that the documents leave out. But specifications are what exam boards and publishers build on, so a gap there tends to carry downstream.

## What the authors say it means

The researchers point to what they call a "compelling" correlation between the gender of the scientists students meet at KS4 and the subjects girls choose at KS5. Girls generally outperform boys in STEM at KS4. At KS5, though, boys are far more likely to take physics, maths and further maths. The share of girls taking further maths is lower than it was in 2005.

The authors are careful about this. Women's underrepresentation in science has many causes, and the study does not show that missing names drive subject choices. The link is a correlation. Physics is the clearest case: the KS4 material is dominated by male scientists, which the authors suggest may play a part in fewer girls continuing with the subject.

## A short fix list

The paper does not call for a rewrite of the curriculum. It asks for small, targeted changes to existing frameworks:

- Include Franklin in all biology specifications that cover DNA structure.
- Include Marie Skłodowska-Curie in KS4 chemistry, in the teaching of atomic structure and isotopes.
- Include Lise Meitner in KS4 physics.
- Include Dorothy Hodgkin in KS5 biology, in the study of protein structure.

White makes the same point about astronomy. Annie Jump Cannon is not mentioned where the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram is taught, although her classification of stars underpins it. "You can't tell one story without the other," she said.

"It is long overdue that we teach these inspiring stories about women," Cooke said. Buttigieg said: "When school science specifications leave out women's names, they miss a real opportunity to help girls see a future for themselves in science."

## What to watch

The fixes are small and the target is easy to check, because a specification either names a scientist or it does not. The coverage seen for this article carried no response from the exam boards. Whether any board adds names at its next specification revision will be the test of whether the findings change anything.

man-utd-como-fernandes-carrick.headline: Man Utd beaten 4-0 by Como as Fernandes rounds on Carrick
man-utd-como-fernandes-carrick.body_md:
Manchester United's captain has questioned the manager's tactics in public. That came hours after the team lost 4-1 at Como in the Champions League on Wednesday night. Bruno Fernandes did not use Michael Carrick's name. He did say the decision not to press man-to-man came from the staff, and he left readers to work out the rest. The result is bad. The question of who is speaking for the dressing room is worse for Carrick.

One correction to the framing circulating on Thursday. The match was not a 4-0 home defeat. Sky Sports and Al Jazeera both report 4-1, played at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia in Como, with Como ahead in the second minute and Joshua Zirkzee scoring a stoppage-time consolation for United. One outlet gave 4-0, which conflicts with every other account found.

## A night that began in the second minute

United went into the game without a win in six matches in all competitions. They had not won since beating Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford on 10 September. Sunday's 1-1 draw at Leeds had stretched the run. Defeat in Italy made it seven. It also left them with three points from three Champions League games and a second European defeat in that time.

Conceding after two minutes shaped the rest of the evening. Fernandes said it did more than put United behind.

> "Conceding early makes us go into the game with a mood of defeat."

Carrick had no argument with the diagnosis, only with the conduct. "For us to play in that way is not acceptable," he said, adding: "You can't turn it on and off." He also said that "whatever tactics you play, if you don't run back, you ain't going to win." Sky Sports read that as the manager questioning his players' motivation. Al Jazeera's account has him taking the blame instead: "I'll take responsibility for the overall team and performance; it stops with me, and I'm fine with that." He also apologised for the performance. The two accounts are not contradictory. A manager can accept the blame and still say the players did not run back, but the order in which he said each thing will matter to how it is received.

## What Fernandes actually said

Fernandes went further than a captain usually does on the night of a heavy defeat. He said the team had not applied enough pressure, and that it was "a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man", leaving some space in behind. Asked directly whether he was criticising Carrick's tactics, he stepped back: "That's on the manager and on the staff to see it, it's not on me."

That answer is the interesting part. He assigned responsibility for the plan to the touchline and then declined to own the criticism. It is the language of a player who wants the point on the record without the headline that follows. The headlines followed anyway: Goal led with "Not brave enough", and Yahoo Sports with "rounds on Carrick".

The contrast with September matters. Fernandes spoke warmly of Carrick earlier in the season, saying the manager had come in with the right ideas and had given the players responsibility and freedom on the pitch. That freedom is now part of the problem. Carrick's line that the players did not run back and Fernandes's line that the staff chose the pressing scheme are two accounts of the same failure, and each puts the fault with the other side.

## The authority question

The case for a squad split rests on thin evidence. It is one captain, one interview, and a sentence he partly retreated from. Nothing in the reporting so far shows other senior players backing him, and Carrick has not responded to Fernandes by name. The BBC was the only source in the original brief. Sky Sports and Al Jazeera now corroborate the substance, but not the 4-0 scoreline.

What can be said is narrower and still uncomfortable for Carrick. He is a former United midfielder who took the job permanently in a season that opened well, and he now has a seven-game winless run, a captain publicly distancing himself from the game plan, and his own comments about effort. When a manager and his captain describe the same defeat in terms that do not meet, the dressing room hears both.

## What comes next

The test comes quickly. United host Bournemouth in the Premier League on Sunday 25 October, and Carrick will face the press beforehand. Whether Fernandes starts, and whether he is asked to repeat or clarify his comments, will say more than either man's words on Wednesday night. After that comes a home Champions League game against Roma. A fourth league win on the board would calm things. Another defeat would turn a remark about pressing into a question about whether Carrick still has the room.

waitrose-new-store-north-london.headline: Waitrose opens first new supermarket in eight years
waitrose-new-store-north-london.body_md:
The north London postcode of NW2 is about to get a Waitrose. The John Lewis Partnership's grocer is opening a new supermarket there, its first in eight years. For a chain that built its name on the well-heeled high street, it ends a long stretch spent refitting what it already had.

The store is reported to be around 18,000 sq ft, a full-size supermarket rather than one of the compact "Little Waitrose" convenience shops that have made up much of the chain's recent footprint. Details such as the exact address and opening date could not be confirmed ahead of filing, and Waitrose should be asked for both.

## Why the pause matters

Waitrose has spent the intervening years tending its estate rather than growing it. The grocer has said it plans to refurbish some 80 stores through to 2028, and to start opening new supermarkets again for the first time in almost a decade. Its recent north London activity has been a rebuild rather than a launch: the John Barnes shop on Finchley Road reopened in August 2024 as a test of a new store concept, the second of its kind after Sudbury, which opened in November 2023.

A fresh site in NW2 suggests those trials have satisfied management that the format is worth taking to new ground. That is an inference from the sequence of events, not something the company has stated.

A second full-line supermarket is also planned, at Brabazon in Bristol, expected in 2027. Taken together the two sites mark a modest but real change of direction.

## A small item, with a limit

There is little here for investors. The John Lewis Partnership is employee-owned and has no listed shares, so a single opening carries no direct market consequence. Its interest is as a read on a mature grocery sector, where the big chains have mostly been closing or reshaping stores rather than building them, and where a premium brand deciding to add floor space says something about its confidence in the customer.

What to watch next is the opening date itself, and whether the Brabazon scheme in Bristol keeps to its 2027 timetable. Two openings in as many years would make a pattern of what is, for now, a single store in a London postcode.

orangutans-laughter-food.headline: Orangutans prefer food linked to the sound of laughter, study suggests
orangutans-laughter-food.body_md:
Play a recording of laughter to an orangutan while it roots through a bowl for food, and it will later favour the bowl's contents. That, in outline, is the finding of a new study of captive apes. It suggests that the sound of play does more than signal fun. It may tilt how an animal values the things around it.

The work, published on 21 October in *Biology Letters* under the title "Play vocalizations induce affective bias in reward learning and memory in orangutans", was led by Daan Laméris, a postdoctoral researcher at Indiana University, with Erica Cartmill, a professor at IU Bloomington. It was first reported by the Guardian.

## How the test worked

The experiment ran over five consecutive days. Orangutans dug through materials in two bowls to find food. On the first and third days, food always lay under one material, wood chips, and never under another, paper towels. On the second and fourth days, the unrewarded material was paired with a new one, yarn, that did cover food.

The key manipulation was sound. While the animals searched in one material, recordings of orangutan laughter played. While they searched in the other, a control sound played. On day five the researchers offered a choice between the two previously rewarded materials. The orangutans preferred the one they had searched through while hearing laughter.

The researchers read this as an "affective bias". Laughter, they argue, puts the animals in a more positive mood. That mood, in turn, raises the value placed on a reward encountered at the time. The effect is familiar from human psychology, where a good mood during an experience can colour how it is remembered.

## Why laughter, and why orangutans

Laughter-like play vocalisations are well documented in great apes, and a bonobo study reported in Scientific Reports found that animals hearing laughter were more willing to chase uncertain rewards. Orangutans are a less obvious subject. "It is surprising to find these effects with orangutans, because they are the least social of all the great apes," Laméris said.

Cartmill framed the wider point more broadly: "What we've shown in this study is that we can measure the value of laughter."

## What is not yet clear

There are reasons for restraint. The university's press release does not state how many orangutans took part. Secondary coverage of the Guardian report describes six animals from two zoos, of which four showed the preference, but that detail could not be checked against the paper itself. Samples of that size are common in primate work, where subjects are scarce, but they limit how far a result can be generalised. The study also shows a preference after a pairing. It does not show what the animals felt, which is inferred from behaviour.

The sound of laughter is also not isolated from other things, such as novelty or arousal, unless the control sound is well matched. The paper's methods will show how closely it was.

## What to watch

The obvious next steps are replication with larger groups and other ape species, and tests of whether the effect depends on laughter specifically or on any positive social sound. For now it stands as a small, tidy signal that the line between emotion, memory and valuation runs through the great apes too.

graduates-leaving-uk.headline: The graduates leaving the UK for a fresh start abroad
graduates-leaving-uk.body_md:
Britain's newest graduates are doing the sums on a UK career and, in growing numbers, deciding the answer lies elsewhere. A survey of 15,000 final-year students found that more than one in ten now plan to move abroad after finishing their degrees, up from 7.8% two years earlier. The BBC reported the trend this week.

The survey is the sturdiest figure in the story, and it measures intent, not departures. Nobody can say from it how many will actually board the plane.

## A crowded queue

The push is easy to see. The Institute of Student Employers puts the average at 140 applications for every graduate vacancy, up 14% on 2025 and against roughly 30 twenty years ago. Separate data from the job board Adzuna showed graduate vacancies down about 46% year on year in July, to 8,383 from 15,397. Adzuna is a single commercial platform, not an official count, so it shows direction better than scale. Official figures point the same way: the ONS has put youth unemployment well into double digits this year.

The ONS also gives the demographic backdrop. About two-thirds of British emigrants are aged 16 to 34, and in 2025 some 75,000 more people in that age group left the UK than arrived.

## Three people, three routes

The BBC's examples are a useful reminder that "abroad" is not one place.

Rachel James, 26, from Surrey, left a corporate job in London in 2025 and went to Sydney with no job lined up. She now works in marketing for Fitness First. Her pay fell from £42,000 to £37,000, and she pays about £1,000 a month to share a two-bedroom flat, roughly what she paid in London. She said she "went for a fresh start".

Charlie West, 25, from Cheshire, took a different path: a funded six-year PhD at Yale after an Oxford master's. His stipend is $51,000 (£37,770), against about £21,000 for funded doctoral stipends in the UK.

Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is finishing a design master's at Aalto University in Finland and lives in Espoo, 15 minutes by metro from Helsinki. Finland's job market is soft, he said, but IT demand is high, and he has no plans to come back soon.

Australia is the most popular destination for British adults overall, helped by a working holiday visa open to UK passport holders aged 18 to 35 for up to three years. The US is second; the EU remains attractive, if harder to enter since Brexit.

## Rational, not romantic

John Kiely, an immigration lawyer at Howard Kennedy, told the BBC that student debt, high housing costs, weak wage growth and job insecurity make leaving a rational choice for many graduates. The pay evidence in the profiles is mixed on that score: Ms James took a cut, while Mr West gained a pay premium.

There is a policy angle too. Graduates who leave take their training with them, a worry Whitehall has voiced before, including during the post-2008 slump. How many return, and when, is the number that would settle whether this is a gap year or a drain. No official series tracks it directly. The next ONS migration estimates and the next High Fliers student survey are the data points to watch.
